lessonTitle: Thyroid, Adrenal and Pituitary Disease: Hormone Excess, Deficiency and Feedback

blocks.text: A 31-year-old woman has lost 8 kg in three months despite eating ravenously. She is sweaty, tremulous, and her heart is racing at 124 beats per minute at rest; her eyes look prominent and her neck is fuller. Her thyroid-stimulating hormone is almost undetectable. One simple blood test pattern, a low pituitary signal with a high gland output, reveals that the thyroid has escaped control.

blocks.markdown: Endocrine glands are usually governed by **negative feedback**: the hormone produced by the target gland inhibits the pituitary and hypothalamic signals that drive it. Disease therefore falls into patterns. A fault at the **target gland** (primary) leaves the pituitary trophic hormone out of step with the gland's output, whereas a fault at the **pituitary or hypothalamus** (secondary or tertiary) makes both move in the same direction.

### The thyroid and its tests

The hypothalamus secretes thyrotropin-releasing hormone (TRH), stimulating pituitary **thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH)**, which drives the thyroid to make thyroxine (T4) and triiodothyronine (T3). Free T4 and T3 feed back to suppress TSH. Thyroid hormones raise metabolic rate and sensitivity to catecholamines, so excess and deficiency cause opposite clinical pictures.

rows: TSH suppressed; free T4 and/or T3 raised
Weight loss despite increased appetite; heat intolerance
Bradycardia, raised diastolic pressure; raised cholesterol
Anxiety, tremor, sweating, warm moist skin
Lethargy, depression, dry skin, hair thinning, slow-relaxing reflexes
Graves disease (TSH-receptor stimulating antibodies); toxic nodule; thyroiditis
Hashimoto thyroiditis (autoimmune); iodine deficiency; after thyroid treatment
blocks.caption: Primary thyroid hormone excess and deficiency (secondary pituitary failure gives low TSH with low free T4)

blocks.title: Reading thyroid function tests
blocks.prompt: A patient has TSH 0.01 mU/L (reference about 0.4-4.0), free T4 38 pmol/L (reference about 12-22) and a diffusely enlarged, non-tender goitre with prominent eyes. Interpret.

steps.text: Free T4 is high, so there is thyroid hormone excess. A normal pituitary would respond by suppressing TSH.
TSH is suppressed, as expected, so the pituitary is responding appropriately and the fault is in the thyroid (primary).
A diffuse goitre with eye signs suggests Graves disease, in which antibodies stimulate the TSH receptor and drive the gland irrespective of TSH.

blocks.answer: Primary hyperthyroidism, most likely Graves disease.

blocks.markdown:
### The pituitary

The **anterior pituitary** secretes TSH, adrenocorticotropic hormone (ACTH), growth hormone, prolactin, and the gonadotropins. Pituitary **adenomas** are common benign tumours. They may secrete a hormone (for example ACTH in Cushing disease, prolactin in prolactinoma) or compress surrounding tissue, causing hypopituitarism and **bitemporal hemianopia** from pressure on the optic chiasm. In **hypopituitarism**, loss of ACTH and TSH produces secondary adrenal and thyroid failure with a low TSH and low free T4.

### The hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal (HPA) axis

The hypothalamus releases **corticotropin-releasing hormone (CRH)**, which stimulates the anterior pituitary to release **ACTH**, which stimulates the adrenal cortex (zona fasciculata) to make **cortisol**. Cortisol, in turn, exerts **negative feedback** on both the pituitary (suppressing ACTH) and the hypothalamus (suppressing CRH). Cortisol follows a diurnal rhythm, highest in the early morning, and rises with stress. This feedback explains the laboratory patterns of disease: autonomous cortisol production (an adrenal tumour) suppresses ACTH, whereas ACTH-driven disease has a high or inappropriately normal ACTH.

blocks.title: Exogenous glucocorticoid and the HPA axis
blocks.prompt: A 50-year-old has taken high-dose oral prednisolone for 6 months for vasculitis and stops it abruptly. Explain why he may collapse with low blood pressure and hypoglycaemia.

steps.text: Prednisolone acts like cortisol, so high levels feed back to suppress hypothalamic CRH and pituitary ACTH.
Without ACTH, the adrenal cortex is not stimulated and atrophies, so it cannot make cortisol when the drug stops.

Cortisol maintains blood pressure (vascular sensitivity to catecholamines) and glucose (gluconeogenesis), so its sudden absence causes adrenal insufficiency with hypotension and hypoglycaemia. Long-term steroids must therefore be tapered.

blocks.answer: Suppressed HPA axis and adrenal atrophy cause adrenal insufficiency when the steroid is stopped suddenly.

rows: Exogenous glucocorticoids (commonest); pituitary ACTH adenoma (Cushing disease); ectopic ACTH (for example small cell lung cancer); adrenal adenoma or carcinoma
Autoimmune adrenalitis (commonest in developed countries); tuberculosis; metastases; haemorrhage
High or normal in pituitary and ectopic disease; suppressed in adrenal tumours
Central obesity, moon face, buffalo hump, purple striae, easy bruising, proximal myopathy, hypertension, hyperglycaemia, osteoporosis
Fatigue, weight loss, hypotension and postural drop, hypoglycaemia, hyponatraemia, hyperkalaemia, skin hyperpigmentation
Fails to suppress cortisol with low-dose dexamethasone
Hyperpigmentation from high ACTH acting on melanocytes (shared POMC precursor with MSH)
blocks.caption: Cushing syndrome and Addison disease compared

blocks.markdown: In primary adrenal failure the cortex also fails to make **aldosterone**, so sodium is lost and potassium retained, explaining hyponatraemia, hyperkalaemia and volume depletion; postural hypotension is defined as a systolic fall of 20 mmHg or more (or diastolic 10 mmHg or more) within 3 minutes of standing. An acute **adrenal crisis** with shock is an emergency that requires urgent glucocorticoid and fluid replacement.

blocks.title: Use feedback to find the level of the lesion
blocks.text: If the target hormone and its trophic hormone move in opposite directions (high T4, low TSH; low cortisol, high ACTH) the lesion is in the target gland. If they move together (low TSH with low T4), the lesion is in the pituitary or hypothalamus.

points: Primary hypothyroidism shows high TSH with low free T4 (Hashimoto thyroiditis is a leading cause), and primary hyperthyroidism shows suppressed TSH with high free T4 (Graves disease is a leading cause).

Cushing syndrome is cortisol excess, most often from exogenous steroids, and Addison disease is primary adrenal failure, most often autoimmune, with hyperpigmentation, hyponatraemia and hyperkalaemia.
Cortisol inhibits CRH and ACTH by negative feedback, so exogenous steroids suppress the axis and cause adrenal atrophy, and the pattern of ACTH and cortisol localises the lesion.

questions.stem: A 45-year-old woman has weight gain, fatigue, cold intolerance and constipation. Her TSH is 62 mU/L (reference about 0.4-4.0) and free T4 is low. What is the most likely cause?

options.text: Autoimmune (Hashimoto) thyroiditis
Graves disease
Pituitary failure
A toxic thyroid adenoma

distractorRationale.a: Correct: a high TSH with low free T4 is primary hypothyroidism, and autoimmune thyroiditis is the commonest cause in iodine-sufficient areas.
distractorRationale.b: Wrong: Graves disease causes hyperthyroidism with suppressed TSH.
distractorRationale.c: Wrong: pituitary failure would give a low or inappropriately normal TSH.
distractorRationale.d: Wrong: a toxic adenoma causes hyperthyroidism.

questions.explanation: The pituitary raises TSH in an attempt to stimulate a failing thyroid, giving a high TSH with low free T4. Autoimmune destruction by Hashimoto thyroiditis is the leading cause.

questions.stem: Which finding best supports Graves disease as the cause of primary hyperthyroidism?

options.text: TSH-receptor stimulating antibodies with a diffuse goitre and eye signs
Raised TSH with raised free T4
Antibodies against thyroid peroxidase with a low free T4
A single nodule with suppressed uptake elsewhere

questions.correctOptionText: TSH-receptor stimulating antibodies with a diffuse goitre and eye signs

distractorRationale.a: Correct: antibodies stimulate the TSH receptor, causing diffuse thyroid enlargement and thyroid eye disease.
distractorRationale.b: Wrong: raised TSH with raised T4 suggests a TSH-secreting pituitary tumour or hormone resistance, not Graves disease.
distractorRationale.d: Wrong: a single autonomously functioning nodule suggests toxic adenoma.

questions.explanation: In Graves disease autoantibodies mimic TSH at its receptor and drive hormone production irrespective of feedback, so TSH is suppressed. The same autoimmune process underlies the diffuse goitre and orbital disease.

questions.stem: Which is the commonest cause of Cushing syndrome overall?

options.text: Exogenous (iatrogenic) glucocorticoid therapy
Pituitary ACTH-secreting adenoma
Adrenal carcinoma
Ectopic ACTH from small cell lung cancer

distractorRationale.a: Correct: prolonged glucocorticoid treatment is the commonest cause.
distractorRationale.b: Wrong: Cushing disease is the commonest endogenous cause but is less common than iatrogenic.

questions.explanation: Many patients take pharmacological doses of steroids for inflammatory conditions, and they develop Cushingoid features. Among endogenous causes, pituitary ACTH-secreting adenoma is the most frequent.

questions.stem: A 40-year-old woman has fatigue, weight loss, postural dizziness and darkened skin creases. Serum sodium is low and potassium high. Which mechanism explains the pigmentation?

options.text: High ACTH from loss of cortisol feedback, acting on melanocytes
Excess cortisol stimulating melanin synthesis
Aldosterone excess
Low ACTH from pituitary failure

questions.correctOptionText: High ACTH from loss of cortisol feedback, acting on melanocytes

distractorRationale.a: Correct: in primary adrenal failure ACTH rises and shares a precursor with melanocyte-stimulating hormone, darkening skin.
distractorRationale.b: Wrong: cortisol is deficient in Addison disease.
distractorRationale.c: Wrong: aldosterone is also deficient, as shown by the low sodium and high potassium.
distractorRationale.d: Wrong: ACTH is high, not low, and pituitary failure does not produce pigmentation.

questions.explanation: Without cortisol feedback, the pituitary releases large amounts of ACTH, cleaved from pro-opiomelanocortin along with melanocyte-stimulating peptides. The result is hyperpigmentation, a clue to primary rather than secondary adrenal failure.

questions.stem: A patient has Cushing syndrome with a high serum cortisol, an undetectable plasma ACTH and a 3 cm adrenal mass on imaging. Which statement explains the low ACTH?

options.text: Autonomous cortisol from the adrenal tumour suppresses CRH and ACTH by negative feedback
The tumour secretes ACTH, which is rapidly degraded
The pituitary is destroyed by the tumour
High cortisol stimulates the pituitary to reduce ACTH only after exercise

questions.correctOptionText: Autonomous cortisol from the adrenal tumour suppresses CRH and ACTH by negative feedback

distractorRationale.a: Correct: cortisol acts on the hypothalamus and pituitary, so high autonomous cortisol suppresses ACTH.
distractorRationale.b: Wrong: ACTH is made by the pituitary or ectopic tumours, not by adrenal adenomas.
distractorRationale.c: Wrong: the pituitary is functionally suppressed, not destroyed.
distractorRationale.d: Wrong: negative feedback acts continuously, not only after exercise.

questions.explanation: Cortisol inhibits CRH and ACTH secretion. An adrenal tumour producing cortisol independently of ACTH therefore drives ACTH down, while the other causes show a high or normal ACTH.

questions.stem: In a dexamethasone suppression test, a patient's morning serum cortisol is 480 nmol/L before and 60 nmol/L after dexamethasone. By what percentage has cortisol fallen?
questions.explanation: The fall is 480 - 60 = 420 nmol/L, and 420 / 480 = 0.875, or 87.5%. Such marked suppression shows an intact negative feedback loop, which argues against Cushing syndrome.

questions.stem: A patient with suspected adrenal insufficiency has a supine blood pressure of 118/76 mmHg and, after 3 minutes standing, 92/60 mmHg. Calculate the fall in systolic pressure in mmHg.
questions.explanation: Systolic pressure fell by 118 - 92 = 26 mmHg, exceeding the 20 mmHg criterion for postural hypotension. In Addison disease this reflects volume depletion from loss of aldosterone and cortisol.

questions.stem: Compare primary hypothyroidism with hyperthyroidism in terms of clinical features and thyroid function tests, naming one common cause of each.
markingGuide: Hypothyroidism: raised TSH with low free T4
Hyperthyroidism: suppressed TSH with raised free T4 or T3
Hypothyroid features: weight gain, cold intolerance, fatigue, constipation, bradycardia, dry skin, menorrhagia
Hyperthyroid features: weight loss, heat intolerance, tremor, tachycardia, anxiety, diarrhoea, sweating
Causes: Hashimoto thyroiditis for hypothyroidism; Graves disease for hyperthyroidism
questions.explanation: Thyroid hormones raise metabolic rate and adrenergic sensitivity, so deficiency and excess produce opposite pictures. In primary disease the TSH moves in the opposite direction to free T4.

questions.stem: Describe the causes and clinical features of Cushing syndrome and of Addison disease, and explain why potassium and sodium are abnormal in Addison disease.
markingGuide: Cushing causes: exogenous steroids, pituitary adenoma, ectopic ACTH, adrenal tumour
Cushing features: central obesity, moon face, striae, bruising, proximal myopathy, hypertension, hyperglycaemia, osteoporosis
Addison causes: autoimmune adrenalitis, tuberculosis, metastases or haemorrhage
Addison features: fatigue, weight loss, postural hypotension, hypoglycaemia, hyperpigmentation
Loss of aldosterone causes sodium loss and potassium retention, so hyponatraemia, hyperkalaemia and volume depletion
questions.explanation: Cushing syndrome reflects excess glucocorticoid action on fat, muscle, skin and bone, whereas Addison disease reflects glucocorticoid and mineralocorticoid deficiency. Aldosterone deficiency explains the electrolyte disturbance and volume depletion.

questions.stem: Describe the hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal axis and its negative feedback. Use it to explain why long-term prednisolone causes adrenal atrophy and why the dose must be tapered rather than stopped suddenly, and how ACTH levels help to separate pituitary from adrenal causes of Cushing syndrome.
markingGuide: CRH from hypothalamus stimulates ACTH from the anterior pituitary, which stimulates cortisol from the adrenal cortex
Cortisol inhibits CRH and ACTH (negative feedback at hypothalamus and pituitary)
Exogenous steroid suppresses CRH and ACTH, so the adrenal cortex atrophies
Sudden withdrawal leaves no endogenous cortisol, causing adrenal insufficiency or crisis
Tapering allows the axis to recover
Adrenal tumour: autonomous cortisol suppresses ACTH (low); pituitary adenoma or ectopic source: ACTH high or normal
questions.explanation: The axis is self-regulating because cortisol restrains its own drivers. Chronic exogenous steroid therefore switches off the drive to the adrenals, and the ACTH level in Cushing syndrome tells whether the excess cortisol is ACTH-dependent.
